claim: Many cellular constituents travel along microtubules in association with multiple copies of motor proteins.
source: Many cellular constituents travel along microtubules in association with multiple copies of motor proteins.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Individual RNPs within a population undergo either diffusive, or highly processive, minus end-directed movements along microtubules.
source: High precision tracking reveals that individual RNPs within a population undergo either diffusive, or highly processive, minus end-directed movements along microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the RAT-TRAP assay and tracking analysis.

claim: RNA localisation signals stimulate the processive movements of RNPs.
source: RNA localisation signals stimulate the processive movements, with regulation of dynein-dynactin's activity rather than its total copy number per RNP, responsible for this effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing different RNA variants (hWT, hΔLE, hSL1x3, HLE).

claim: Regulation of dynein-dynactin's activity rather than its total copy number per RNP is responsible for stimulating processive movements.
source: RNA localisation signals stimulate the processive movements, with regulation of dynein-dynactin's activity rather than its total copy number per RNP, responsible for this effect.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that the HLE alone promotes unidirectional motion despite having similar dynein copy numbers to hΔLE.

claim: Mutations in microtubule motor proteins and their co-factors are associated with several neurological disorders.
source: The significance of this process is underscored by the association of mutations in microtubule motor proteins and their co-factors with several neurological disorders (Hirokawa et al., 2010; Schiavo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many pathogens exploit cellular microtubule motors during infection.
source: Furthermore, many pathogens exploit cellular microtubule motors during infection (Grieshaber et al., 2003; Greber and Way, 2006; Ramsden et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Individual cargos simultaneously associate with multiple microtubule motors.
source: There is substantial evidence that individual cargos simultaneously associate with multiple microtubule motors (Gross et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A single cargo can associate with several copies of the same kind of motor.
source: Not only can a single cargo associate with several copies of the same kind of motor (e.g., Leopold et al., 1992; Welte et al., 1998; Hendricks et al., 2010; Encalada et al., 2011; Rai et al., 2013), but opposite polarity motors are often stably bound (Ling et al., 2004; Pilling et al., 2006; Shubeita et al., 2008; Soppina et al., 2009; Hendricks et al., 2010; Encalada et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Opposite polarity motors are often stably bound to a single cargo.
source: Not only can a single cargo associate with several copies of the same kind of motor (e.g., Leopold et al., 1992; Welte et al., 1998; Hendricks et al., 2010; Encalada et al., 2011; Rai et al., 2013), but opposite polarity motors are often stably bound (Ling et al., 2004; Pilling et al., 2006; Shubeita et al., 2008; Soppina et al., 2009; Hendricks et al., 2010; Encalada et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Small increases in the number of purified motors of the same polarity strongly augment the average travel distance in that direction.
source: These in vitro studies have provided evidence that small increases in the number of purified motors of the same polarity strongly augment the average travel distance in that direction (Block et al., 1990; Mallik et al., 2005; Vershinin et al., 2007; Derr et al., 2012; Furuta et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The plus end-directed kinesin-1 motor frequently detaches when encountering microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs).
source: In vitro experiments have shown that the plus end-directed kinesin-1 motor frequently detaches when encountering microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) (Vershinin et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2008; Telley et al., 2009; McVicker et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Individual bidirectional dynein-dynactins often remain attached to a microtubule and undergo a reversal in travel direction upon encountering an obstacle.
source: In contrast, upon such an obstacle encounter, individual bidirectional dynein-dynactins often remain attached to a microtubule and undergo a reversal in travel direction (Dixit et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Apical mRNA localisation is achieved by a bidirectional translocation process in which minus end-directed transport by dynein-dynactin predominates.
source: These experiments have provided evidence that apical mRNA localisation is achieved by a bidirectional translocation process in which, on average, minus end-directed transport by the multi-subunit dynein motor and its large accessory complex dynactin predominates (Wilkie and Davis, 2001; Bullock et al., 2006; Vendra et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: RNPs are statically anchored in the apical cytoplasm by an unknown, dynein-dependent mechanism.
source: Upon reaching the apical cytoplasm, the ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNPs) are statically anchored by an unknown, dynein-dependent mechanism (Delanoue and Davis, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Dynein-dynactin is required for both plus end- and minus end-directed motion of localising and uniformly distributed RNPs.
source: Intriguingly, dynein-dynactin is required for both plus end- and minus end-directed motion of the localising and uniformly distributed RNPs formed upon injection (Bullock et al., 2006; Vendra et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dynein is needed for efficient spreading of uniformly distributed endogenous RNAs from the perinuclear region.
source: Dynein is also needed for efficient spreading of uniformly distributed endogenous RNAs from the perinuclear region, supporting a physiological requirement for the motor complex in bidirectional RNA motion (Bullock et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Plus end movements of RNPs are driven by dynein moving in this direction.
source: These findings, together with the failure to detect functional evidence for the involvement of a kinesin motor (Vendra et al., 2007), suggest that plus end movements of RNPs are driven by dynein moving in this direction, a property that has been documented in several in vitro studies of the motor (Schliwa et al., 1991; Wang et al., 1995; Wang and Sheetz, 2000; Mallik et al., 2005; Ross et al., 2006; Miura et al., 2010; Walter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and inference from experimental observations.

claim: Net minus end transport of apical transcripts is dependent on RNA localisation signals.
source: Net minus end transport of apical transcripts is dependent on RNA localisation signals, which are comprised of specialised stem-loops that recruit additional dynein-dynactin complexes to RNPs through the Egalitarian (Egl) and Bicaudal-D (BicD) adaptor proteins (Bullock et al., 2006; Dienstbier et al., 2009; Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Egl binds directly to the localisation signals.
source: Egl binds directly to the localisation signals (Dienstbier et al., 2009) and the light chain subunit of dynein (Navarro et al., 2004), whereas BicD interacts simultaneously with Egl (Navarro et al., 2004; Dienstbier et al., 2009) and multiple sites in the dynein-dynactin complex (Hoogenraad et al., 2001; Splinter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BicD interacts simultaneously with Egl and multiple sites in the dynein-dynactin complex.
source: Egl binds directly to the localisation signals (Dienstbier et al., 2009) and the light chain subunit of dynein (Navarro et al., 2004), whereas BicD interacts simultaneously with Egl (Navarro et al., 2004; Dienstbier et al., 2009) and multiple sites in the dynein-dynactin complex (Hoogenraad et al., 2001; Splinter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Egl and BicD do not appear to contribute to the binding of the dynein-dynactin complex to RNA at sites other than localisation signals.
source: Egl and BicD do not appear to contribute to the binding of the dynein-dynactin complex to RNA at sites other than localisation signals (Bullock et al., 2006; Dix et al., 2013), and the RNA features and protein factors that fulfil this task have not been identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lissencephaly-1 (Lis1) is a component of dynein-dynactin complexes associated with localising and uniformly distributed RNAs.
source: Recent proteomic work by our group (Dix et al., 2013) has shown that Lissencephaly-1 (Lis1) is also a component of dynein-dynactin complexes associated with localising and uniformly distributed RNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Lis1 promotes the recruitment of dynein-dynactin to RNAs.
source: Lis1 promotes the recruitment of dynein-dynactin to RNAs (Dix et al., 2013) and may also regulate mechanochemistry of the cargo-associated motor (McKenney et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2012; Vallee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lis1 may regulate mechanochemistry of the cargo-associated motor.
source: Lis1 promotes the recruitment of dynein-dynactin to RNAs (Dix et al., 2013) and may also regulate mechanochemistry of the cargo-associated motor (McKenney et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2012; Vallee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and is presented as speculative.

claim: A core functional complex recruited to localisation signals consists of Egl, BicD, dynein-dynactin, and Lis1.
source: The study of Dix et al. supported the existence of a core functional complex recruited to localisation signals, consisting of Egl, BicD, dynein-dynactin, and Lis1 (Dix et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: 50–80 microtubule-associated RNPs were typically observed following injection of the eluate into an imaging chamber.
source: 50–80 microtubule-associated RNPs were typically observed following injection of the eluate into an imaging chamber, with ∼60–70% of these displaying motility during the ∼100 s of data acquisition.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RAT-TRAP assay experiments.

claim: ∼60–70% of microtubule-associated RNPs displayed motility during the ∼100 s of data acquisition.
source: 50–80 microtubule-associated RNPs were typically observed following injection of the eluate into an imaging chamber, with ∼60–70% of these displaying motility during the ∼100 s of data acquisition.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the RAT-TRAP assay experiments.

claim: There was a strong overall minus end bias to motility of the hWT RNP population.
source: There was a strong overall minus end bias to motility of the hWT RNP population, as is the case in vivo (Bullock et al., 2003, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the RAT-TRAP assay and citations to in vivo observations.

claim: 24 ± 1% of motile hWT RNPs analysed per chamber moved exclusively unidirectionally towards the minus ends of microtubules.
source: 24 ± 1% of motile RNPs analysed per chamber moved exclusively unidirectionally towards the minus ends of microtubules (mean ± SEM, 10 chambers; e.g., Figure 1B,D; Video 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RAT-TRAP assay experiments, with reference to figures and video.

claim: Unidirectional hWT RNP movements were highly processive, often ending when RNPs paused or detached upon reaching the microtubule minus end.
source: These movements were highly processive, often ending when RNPs paused or detached upon reaching the microtubule minus end.
evidence: This is an observation from the RAT-TRAP assay experiments.

claim: The remainder of motile hWT RNPs moved bidirectionally, with frequent switches in direction.
source: The remainder of motile hWT RNPs moved bidirectionally, with frequent switches in direction (e.g., Figure 1C,E; Video 2) and no overt directional bias at the population level (see below for quantification).
evidence: This is an observation from the RAT-TRAP assay experiments, with reference to figures and video.

claim: Endogenous h RNPs contain a single copy of the RNA molecule.
source: We have recently shown that, unlike the large RNPs formed after injection of fluorescent RNA into the embryo, endogenous h RNPs contain a single copy of the RNA molecule (Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: All motile RNPs assembled with equimolar Alexa488-labelled h and Cy3-labelled h contained only one type of fluorophore.
source: All motile RNPs assembled in such experiments contained only one type of fluorophore (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: The RAT-TRAP assay reports on the motility of RNPs containing a single fluorescent RNA molecule.
source: These data indicate that, as was the case for our previous in vitro assay for RNA motility (Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012), the RAT-TRAP assay reports on the motility of RNPs containing a single fluorescent RNA molecule.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and comparison to previous work.

claim: The number of motile hWT RNPs observed in RAT-TRAP assays was ∼10-fold greater than that observed using the previous method.
source: The number of motile hWT RNPs observed in RAT-TRAP assays was ∼10-fold greater than that observed using our previous method ([Amrute-Nayak and Bullock, 2012] and data not shown).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results between the new and previous methods.

claim: Unidirectional hWT RNP trajectories showed a quadratic dependence of mean square displacement (MSD) over time.
source: As expected, unidirectional hWT RNP trajectories showed a quadratic dependence of mean square displacement (MSD) over time (average slope of ∼2.0 in a log–log plot [Figure 2A]; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C for additional MSD analysis).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from MSD analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Quadratic dependence of MSD over time indicates an underlying active transport process.
source: This observation indicates an underlying active transport process (Saxton, 1997; Sanchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MSD data supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The relationship of MSD of bidirectional hWT RNPs over time was linear.
source: In contrast, the relationship of MSD of bidirectional RNPs over time was linear (average slope of ∼1.0 in the log–log plot (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from MSD analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Linear relationship of MSD over time indicates a strong diffusive component to the movement.
source: Thus, there appears to be a strong diffusive component to the movement of bidirectional hWT RNPs (Saxton, 1997; Sanchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the MSD data supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mean length of individual runs of unidirectional hWT RNPs was ∼4 μm.
source: The mean length and velocity of individual runs of unidirectional hWT RNPs were ∼4 μm and ∼1.2 μm.s−1, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from run analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The mean velocity of individual runs of unidirectional hWT RNPs was ∼1.2 μm.s−1.
source: The mean length and velocity of individual runs of unidirectional hWT RNPs were ∼4 μm and ∼1.2 μm.s−1, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from run analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The mean velocity of individual runs of bidirectional hWT RNPs in both directions was ∼0.8 μm.s−1.
source: The mean velocity of individual runs of bidirectional hWT RNPs in both directions (∼0.8 μm.s−1) was similar to that of the unidirectional counterparts, whereas the mean run lengths were much shorter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from run analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The mean length of individual runs of bidirectional hWT RNPs in both directions was ∼120 nm.
source: In both directions the mean length of individual runs of bidirectional RNPs was ∼120 nm; only a small fraction of runs were longer than 500 nm, with the longest ∼2 μm (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and accompanying legend).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from run analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The run lengths of bidirectional hWT RNPs are much shorter than those previously documented for force-generating dynein and kinesin motors bound to other bidirectional cargos.
source: These run lengths are much shorter than those previously documented for force-generating dynein and kinesin motors bound to other bidirectional cargos (Shubeita et al., 2008; Soppina et al., 2009; Schuster et al., 2011; Reis et al., 2012; Rai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results to published literature.

claim: The mean minus end and plus end run lengths were very similar for any given bidirectional hWT RNP.
source: The mean minus end and plus end run lengths were very similar for any given RNP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Individual bidirectional hWT RNPs exhibited mean velocities that were highly similar in both the minus end and plus end direction.
source: Individual RNPs also exhibited mean velocities that were highly similar in both the minus end and plus end direction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Mean run lengths and run velocities for individual bidirectional hWT RNPs were highly correlated.
source: Mean run lengths and run velocities for individual RNPs were also highly correlated (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Complexes that move faster on average tended to move further before a run ends.
source: Thus, complexes that move faster on average tended to move further before a run ends.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis.

claim: Depletion of ATP and ADP with apyrase led to a significant increase in the number of microtubule-associated hWT RNPs compared to the ATP condition.
source: Depletion of ATP and ADP with apyrase (Higuchi et al., 1997; Ma and Taylor, 1997) led to a significant increase in the number of microtubule-associated RNPs compared to the ATP condition (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure and citations for the apyrase method.

claim: In the presence of apyrase there was a large increase in the proportion of microtubule-bound hWT RNPs that were stationary.
source: In the presence of apyrase there was also a large increase in the proportion of microtubule-bound RNPs that were stationary, with unidirectional behaviour absent and a strong reduction in the proportion of bidirectional complexes (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Unidirectional behaviour was absent in the presence of apyrase.
source: In the presence of apyrase there was also a large increase in the proportion of microtubule-bound RNPs that were stationary, with unidirectional behaviour absent and a strong reduction in the proportion of bidirectional complexes (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Processive movement of dynein is dependent on ATP hydrolysis.
source: The affect of apyrase on unidirectional motion is entirely expected as processive movement of dynein is dependent on ATP hydrolysis (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There was a partial reduction in the number of hWT RNPs bound to microtubules in the presence of vanadate.
source: There was a partial reduction in the number of RNPs bound to microtubules in the presence of vanadate (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Vanadate abolished unidirectional motion of the microtubule-associated hWT RNPs.
source: As expected, vanadate abolished unidirectional motion of the microtubule-associated RNPs (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The percentage of microtubule-associated hWT RNPs that underwent bidirectional motion was not decreased in the presence of ATP-vanadate compared to ATP alone.
source: Tellingly, the percentage of microtubule-associated RNPs that underwent bidirectional motion was not decreased in the presence of ATP-vanadate compared to ATP alone (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The relationship of MSD vs time was very similar for the bidirectional hWT RNPs in the presence of ATP-vanadate and ATP.
source: The relationship of MSD vs time was very similar for the bidirectional RNPs in the presence of ATP-vanadate and ATP (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from MSD analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Similar distributions of lengths and velocities of individual runs in both the minus and plus end direction were observed for bidirectional hWT RNPs in both ATP and ATP-vanadate conditions.
source: Similar distributions of lengths and velocities or individual runs in both the minus and plus end direction were also observed for bidirectional RNPs in both conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Even the occurrence of relatively long runs of hWT RNPs was not prevented by vanadate.
source: Thus, even the occurrence of relatively long runs of hWT RNPs was not prevented by vanadate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Vanadate caused a subtle but statistically significant increase in the mean run length and velocity of bidirectional hWT RNPs in the minus and plus end directions.
source: Vanadate actually caused a subtle but statistically significant increase in the mean run length and velocity of bidirectional RNPs in the minus and plus end directions (Figure 2H,I), implying a modulation of the diffusive properties of RNPs when dynein is in the ADP.Pi state.
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: An active energy transduction property of dynein is required for unidirectional, minus end-directed RNP motion but not for motion of bidirectional RNPs in either the minus or plus end direction.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that an active energy transduction property of dynein is required for unidirectional, minus end-directed RNP motion but not for motion of bidirectional RNPs in either the minus or plus end direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with apyrase and vanadate.

claim: Individual hWT RNPs can adopt two discrete behaviours in vitro: unidirectional motion, driven by processive movement of dynein that is associated with ATP hydrolysis and bidirectional motion that appears to be dominated by passive diffusion.
source: Thus, individual hWT RNPs can adopt two discrete behaviours in vitro: unidirectional motion, driven by processive movement of dynein that is associated with ATP hydrolysis and bidirectional motion that appears to be dominated by passive diffusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The key feature of the HLE is stem-loop 1 (SL1).
source: The key feature of the HLE is stem-loop 1 (SL1) (Bullock et al., 2003), which recruits dynein-dynactin through the adaptor proteins Egl and BicD (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Dix et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SL1 recruits dynein-dynactin through the adaptor proteins Egl and BicD.
source: The key feature of the HLE is stem-loop 1 (SL1) (Bullock et al., 2003), which recruits dynein-dynactin through the adaptor proteins Egl and BicD (Dienstbier et al., 2009; Dix et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Manipulating SL1 copy number in the different h RNA variants causes significant changes, in relative terms, in the average copy number of dynein and dynactin complexes per RNP.
source: Nonetheless, our analysis clearly reveals that manipulating SL1 copy number in the different h RNA variants causes significant changes, in relative terms, in the average copy number of dynein and dynactin complexes per RNP.
evidence: This is a conclusion from stepwise photobleaching experiments.

claim: The estimated means ± SEM of Dlic copies for hWT, hΔLE, and hSL1x3 RNPs were, respectively, 6.73 ± 0.44, 4.36 ± 0.33, and 13.85 ± 0.67.
source: The estimated means ± SEM of Dlic copies for hWT, hΔLE, and hSL1x3 RNPs were, respectively, 6.73 ± 0.44, 4.36 ± 0.33, and 13.85 ± 0.67.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from photobleaching analysis.

claim: There are two Dlic molecules per dynein motor.
source: It has been reported that there are two Dlic molecules per dynein motor (King et al., 1996; Trokter et al., 2012) and hence our estimates of Dlic copy number on h RNA variants are consistent with 3.36 ± 0.21, 2.18 ± 0.16, and 6.92 ± 0.33 dynein motors associated with hWT, hΔLE, or hSL1x3 RNPs, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The estimates of Dlic copy number on h RNA variants are consistent with 3.36 ± 0.21, 2.18 ± 0.16, and 6.92 ± 0.33 dynein motors associated with hWT, hΔLE, or hSL1x3 RNPs, respectively.
source: It has been reported that there are two Dlic molecules per dynein motor (King et al., 1996; Trokter et al., 2012) and hence our estimates of Dlic copy number on h RNA variants are consistent with 3.36 ± 0.21, 2.18 ± 0.16, and 6.92 ± 0.33 dynein motors associated with hWT, hΔLE, or hSL1x3 RNPs, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculation based on photobleaching data and published information about Dlic stoichiometry.

claim: The population of hSL1x3 RNPs had a significantly greater minus end-directed bias than the hWT RNPs.
source: The population of hSL1x3 RNPs had a significantly greater minus end-directed bias than the hWT RNPs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: There was a doubling in the proportion of motile hSL1x3 RNPs undergoing exclusively unidirectional movement towards the minus end of microtubules compared to hWT RNPs.
source: This was associated with a doubling in the proportion of motile hSL1x3 RNPs undergoing exclusively unidirectional movement towards the minus end of microtubules compared to hWT RNPs (Figure 3E), without substantially altering the mean run lengths and velocities of these events (Figure 3F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Reducing the copy number of dynein-dynactin per RNP by using the hΔLE RNA resulted in exclusively bidirectional motion.
source: Reducing the copy number of dynein-dynactin per RNP by using the hΔLE RNA resulted in exclusively bidirectional motion (Figure 3E) with no significant net directional bias (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: There was a correlation between the probability of unidirectional minus end-directed motion of RNPs and the average number of associated dynein-dynactin complexes.
source: Thus, there was a correlation between the probability of unidirectional minus end-directed motion of RNPs and the average number of associated dynein-dynactin complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with different RNA variants.

claim: The distribution of run lengths and velocities of the bidirectional RNPs in the minus and plus end directions were similar for hWT, hSL1x3, and hΔLE RNAs.
source: The distribution of run lengths and velocities of the bidirectional RNPs in the minus and plus end directions were similar for hWT, hSL1x3, and hΔLE RNAs (Figure 3H,I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: There was a subtle increase in both minus and plus end mean run lengths and velocities with increasing numbers of SL1 elements.
source: There was, however, a subtle increase in both minus and plus end mean run lengths and velocities with increasing numbers of SL1 elements (Figure 3H,I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Increasing dynein-dynactin copy number through localisation signals does not have a major influence on the motile properties of bidirectional RNPs.
source: These data suggest that increasing dynein-dynactin copy number through localisation signals does not have a major influence on the motile properties of bidirectional RNPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The correlation between increased dynein-dynactin number and increased lengths and velocities of runs in both the minus and plus end direction is consistent with this complex playing a direct role in mediating bidirectional movement of RNPs along microtubules.
source: However, the correlation between increased dynein-dynactin number and increased lengths and velocities of runs in both the minus and plus end direction is consistent with this complex playing a direct role in mediating bidirectional movement of RNPs along microtubules.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Individual purified dynein-dynactin complexes move bidirectionally in vitro, with additional dynein-dynactin complexes bound to a bead driving unidirectional motion in the minus end direction.
source: Such a model is consistent with previous work showing that individual purified dynein-dynactin complexes move bidirectionally in vitro, with additional dynein-dynactin complexes bound to a bead driving unidirectional motion in the minus end direction (Ross et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the relative copy number of the motor complex on HLE RNPs compared to hWT RNPs.
source: Importantly, we first confirmed using stepwise photobleaching with GFP-Dlic extracts that there is a significant reduction in the relative copy number of the motor complex on HLE RNPs compared to hWT RNPs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental result from photobleaching analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: The average number of GFP::Dlic photobleaching steps on the HLE was statistically indistinguishable from that observed for hΔLE.
source: The average number of GFP::Dlic photobleaching steps on the HLE was in fact statistically indistinguishable from that observed for hΔLE (2.21 ± 0.15 and 2.14 ± 0.16, respectively; Figure 4A and Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from photobleaching analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Approximately 65% of RNPs containing the HLE RNA exhibited unidirectional motion towards the minus end of microtubules, compared to 24% of those containing the hWT RNA.
source: However, this was not the case. Approximately 65% of RNPs containing the HLE RNA exhibited unidirectional motion towards the minus end of microtubules, compared to 24% of those containing the hWT RNA (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The HLE RNP population had a particularly strong minus end directional bias.
source: Consequently, the HLE RNP population had a particularly strong minus end directional bias (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Total dynein-dynactin copy number is not the primary determinant of unidirectional RNP movement.
source: These data indicate that total dynein-dynactin copy number is not the primary determinant of unidirectional RNP movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results with HLE and hΔLE RNAs.

claim: The HLE promotes the ability of the associated dynein-dynactin to undergo unidirectional transport, with features in the rest of the 3′UTR seemingly antagonising this effect.
source: Instead the HLE promotes the ability of the associated dynein-dynactin to undergo unidirectional transport, with features in the rest of the 3′UTR seemingly antagonising this effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The mean run lengths and velocities of unidirectional runs of HLE RNPs were indistinguishable from those of hWT RNPs.
source: The mean run lengths and velocities of unidirectional runs of HLE RNPs were indistinguishable from those of hWT RNPs ((Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D); note that in this series of experiments, and others involving the HLE, the image exposure time was increased (acquisition rate, 4.2 fps) to compensate for the reduced number of Cy3 dyes incorporated into the shorter RNA.
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Once initiated the unidirectional mode of transport is not strongly influenced by the average number of cargo-associated dynein-dynactins.
source: The comparison of unidirectional runs of HLE and hWT RNPs, together with the earlier evaluation of unidirectional motility of hSL1x3 and hWT RNPs (Figure 3F,G), demonstrates that once initiated the unidirectional mode of transport is not strongly influenced by the average number of cargo-associated dynein-dynactins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The bidirectional HLE RNPs exhibited similar mean lengths and velocities of individual runs in both the minus and plus end directions and these were no greater than those of the bidirectional subset of hWT RNPs.
source: The bidirectional HLE RNPs exhibited similar mean lengths and velocities of individual runs in both the minus and plus end directions and these were no greater than those of the bidirectional subset of hWT RNPs (Figure 4F,G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: The dynein-dynactin recruited specifically by RNA localisation signals determines the likelihood of RNPs initiating an exclusively unidirectional, minus end-directed mode of transport but is not sufficient to cause an increase in the length or velocity of excursions of bidirectional RNPs in either direction.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that the dynein-dynactin recruited specifically by RNA localisation signals determines the likelihood of RNPs initiating an exclusively unidirectional, minus end-directed mode of transport but is not sufficient to cause an increase in the length or velocity of excursions of bidirectional RNPs in either direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The presence of kin401T99N:mGFP on microtubules led to a concentration-dependent decrease in the net minus end directional bias of the hWT RNP population.
source: The presence of kin401T99N:mGFP on microtubules led to a concentration-dependent decrease in the net minus end directional bias of the hWT RNP population (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The presence of tau23 on the microtubules reduced the overall minus end bias to hWT RNP motion.
source: The presence of tau23 on the microtubules also reduced the overall minus end bias to hWT RNP motion (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The effect of the MAPs was not associated with a significant reduction in the time that hWT RNPs were detected in association with microtubules.
source: This effect of the MAPs was not associated with a significant reduction in the time that hWT RNPs were detected in association with microtubules (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Unlike the case for the wild-type kinesin-1 motor under similar conditions, hWT RNPs did not frequently detach from microtubules bound by kin401T99N:mGFP or tau23.
source: Thus, unlike the case for the wild-type kinesin-1 motor under similar conditions (Dixit et al., 2008; Telley et al., 2009; McVicker et al., 2011), hWT RNPs did not frequently detach from microtubules bound by kin401T99N:mGFP or tau23.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results to published literature.

claim: The presence of MAPs appears to alter the motile properties of the RNPs without displacing them from the microtubule.
source: Thus, the presence of these MAPs appears to alter the motile properties of the RNPs without displacing them from the microtubule.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The reduction in net minus end motion of the hWT population in the presence of MAPs was associated with a significant decrease in the proportion of RNPs that moved exclusively unidirectionally towards the minus end of the microtubule.
source: The reduction in net minus end motion of the hWT population in the presence of MAPs was associated with a significant decrease in the proportion of RNPs that moved exclusively unidirectionally towards the minus end of the microtubule (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: No unidirectional hWT RNPs were observed in chambers with the highest concentration of kin401T99N:mGFP.
source: Indeed, no unidirectional hWT RNPs were observed in chambers with the highest concentration of kin401T99N:mGFP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Unidirectional RNPs are capable of switching to a bidirectional mode in response to MAPs.
source: These observations suggest that unidirectional RNPs are capable of switching to a bidirectional mode in response to MAPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Encounters of hWT RNPs with a region of microtubule bound by a kin401T99N:mGFP punctum were rarely associated with RNP detachment or pausing (<5% of encounters in total).
source: Encounters of hWT RNPs with a region of microtubule bound by a kin401T99N:mGFP punctum were rarely associated with RNP detachment or pausing (<5% of encounters in total).
evidence: This is an experimental result.

claim: In approximately 25% of cases, hWT RNPs passed the region bound by a rigor kinesin punctum.
source: In approximately 25% of cases, RNPs passed the region bound by a rigor kinesin punctum (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The vast majority (∼70%) of encounters of hWT RNPs with a region bound by a kin401T99N:mGFP punctum coincided with a reversal of the RNP on the microtubule, regardless of the direction of initial motion.
source: The vast majority (∼70%) of encounters of hWT RNPs with a region bound by a kin401T99N:mGFP punctum coincided with a reversal of the RNP on the microtubule, regardless of the direction of initial motion (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: A much lower incidence of reversals (∼10–15%) was expected by random chance, as revealed by analysing the dataset with simulated MAP positions.
source: A much lower incidence of reversals (∼10–15%) was expected by random chance, as revealed by analysing the dataset with simulated MAP positions (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an experimental result from simulation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Encounters of hWT RNPs with regions of microtubules decorated with static tau23 also led to a reversal in the vast majority of cases, with very few detachments or pauses.
source: Encounters of RNPs with regions of microtubules decorated with static tau23 also led to a reversal in the vast majority of cases, with very few detachments or pauses (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Encounters with MAPs frequently induce reversals of hWT RNPs.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that encounters with MAPs frequently induce reversals of hWT RNPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The correlation between mean minus end and mean plus end travel distance per RNP was reduced in the presence of kin401T99N:mGFP and tau23.
source: Consistent with reversals in these experiments being influenced not just by intrinsic properties of the RNPs but also by the stochastic positioning of MAPs on the microtubule, the correlation between mean minus end and mean plus end travel distance per RNP was reduced in the presence of kin401T99N:mGFP and tau23 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The influence of MAPs may explain why tightly correlated motion of cargo-motor complexes in each direction has not been previously observed in vivo.
source: The influence of MAPs may therefore explain why tightly correlated motion of cargo-motor complexes in each direction has not been previously observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: The proportion of hSL1x3 RNPs that were unidirectional, and hence the overall minus end bias of the population, was reduced in the presence of kin401T99N:mGFP without a significant reduction in the dwell time of RNPs on microtubules.
source: Consistent with what was seen for hWT (Figure 5A–C), the proportion of hSL1x3 RNPs that were unidirectional, and hence the overall minus end bias of the population, was reduced in the presence of the MAP without a significant reduction in the dwell time of RNPs on microtubules (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: ∼70% of encounters of hSL1x3 RNPs with regions of microtubules bound by kin401T99N:mGFP puncta preceded by either minus or plus end-directed motion were associated with a reversal, while detachments and pauses were rare.
source: Analysis of individual encounters of hSL1x3 RNPs with regions of microtubules bound by kin401T99N:mGFP puncta revealed a quantitatively similar behaviour to that observed for hWT RNPs; ∼70% of encounters preceded by either minus or plus end-directed motion were associated with a reversal, while detachments and pauses were rare (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The movement of RNPs containing the short HLE RNA was curtailed by kin401T99N:mGFP, with the proportion of motile RNPs that were unidirectional reduced significantly.
source: The movement of RNPs containing the short HLE RNA was also curtailed by kin401T99N:mGFP, with the proportion of motile RNPs that were unidirectional reduced significantly (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Despite containing fewer associated dynein-dynactins, HLE RNPs reversed at obstacles with similar probability to hWT and hSL1x3 RNPs.
source: Furthermore, despite containing fewer associated dynein-dynactins, HLE RNPs reversed at obstacles with similar probability to hWT and hSL1x3 RNPs (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: The total number of associated dynein-dynactin complexes does not influence the ability of RNPs to navigate around microtubule-associated obstacles.
source: Collectively, this series of experiments indicates that the total number of associated dynein-dynactin complexes does not influence the ability of RNPs to navigate around microtubule-associated obstacles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Encounters of bidirectional hWT RNPs with plus ends always led to a reversal in travel direction.
source: Interestingly, encounters of bidirectional hWT RNPs with plus ends always led to a reversal in travel direction (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Bidirectional hWT RNPs do not detach at the plus end.
source: Thus, these RNPs do not detach at the plus end, a behaviour that might facilitate their long-term translocation on the microtubule cytoskeleton in vivo ('Discussion').
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Reversals of bidirectional hWT RNPs were common upon reaching the minus end, occurring ∼70% of the time.
source: Reversals of bidirectional hWT RNPs were also common upon reaching the minus end, occurring ∼70% of the time (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Detachments of bidirectional hWT RNPs upon immediately reaching a minus end were rare (∼5% of total encounters).
source: Detachments of bidirectional hWT RNPs upon immediately reaching a minus end were rare (∼5% of total encounters) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to a figure.

claim: Approximately 25% of encounters of bidirectional hWT RNPs with minus ends resulted in long-term pausing at this site, with a mean dwell time of ∼1 min.
source: Approximately 25% of encounters of these RNPs with minus ends resulted in long-term pausing at this site, with a mean dwell time of ∼1 min (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Unidirectional hWT RNPs did not reverse at the minus end.
source: By definition, unidirectional hWT RNPs did not reverse at the minus end.
evidence: This is a logical statement based on the definition of unidirectional motion.

claim: No example of a reversal at the minus end was observed that was preceded by a long minus end-directed run (>3 μm).
source: Nonetheless, we never observed an example of a reversal at the minus end that was preceded by a long minus end-directed run (>3 μm).
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: Unidirectional motion does not appear to be followed by a reversal at the minus end.
source: Thus, unidirectional motion does not appear to be followed by a reversal at the minus end.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observation.

claim: Approximately 70% of encounters of unidirectional hWT RNPs with a minus end resulted in pausing, with detachment from the microtubule occurring in all other cases.
source: Approximately 70% of encounters of unidirectional hWT RNPs with a minus end resulted in pausing, with detachment from the microtubule occurring in all other cases (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: hWT RNPs are capable of recognising the minus end of microtubules and being retained there.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that hWT RNPs are capable of recognising the minus end of microtubules and being retained there.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: This process may contribute to the dynein-dependent anchorage of RNAs in the apical cytoplasm that has been observed in vivo.
source: This process may contribute to the dynein-dependent anchorage of RNAs in the apical cytoplasm that has been observed in vivo (Delanoue and Davis, 2005) ('Discussion').
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results and citation to in vivo observations.

claim: Bidirectional RNPs containing hΔLE and hSL1x3 behaved indistinguishably to hWT RNPs at minus and plus ends.
source: Bidirectional RNPs containing these RNA species behaved indistinguishably to hWT RNPs at minus and plus ends (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Unidirectional hSL1x3 RNPs responded to minus ends of microtubules in the same manner as unidirectional hWT RNPs.
source: Unidirectional hSL1x3 RNPs also responded to minus ends of microtubules in the same manner as unidirectional hWT RNPs (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Average dynein-dynactin copy number does not influence the reaction to microtubule ends of RNPs that harbour h 3′UTRs.
source: Thus, average dynein-dynactin copy number does not influence the reaction to microtubule ends of RNPs that harbour h 3′UTRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

source: Interestingly, the mean durations of pauses of unidirectional hWT and hSL1x3 RNPs at minus ends were ∼ fivefold shorter than those exhibited by bidirectional RNPs containing the same RNA species (Figure 6C,F; e.g., hWT unidirectional, 10.7 ± 1.7 s; hWT bidirectional, 58.9 ± 8.0 s (p<0.0001, Mann–Whitney non-parametric t test)).

claim: Features that promote bidirectional motion aid in the retention of RNPs at the minus end.

evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: The duration of pauses of unidirectional HLE RNPs at minus ends was significantly reduced compared to unidirectional hWT and hSL1x3 RNPs.
source: Upon reaching the minus end, unidirectional HLE RNPs were more likely to detach than unidirectional hWT and hSL1x3 RNPs (Figure 6E), and the duration of pauses was significantly reduced (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an experimental result, with reference to figures.

claim: Anchorage of RNPs at minus ends is facilitated by features that promote bidirectional movement.
source: This observation is compatible with the notion that anchorage of RNPs at minus ends is facilitated by features that promote bidirectional movement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The RAT-TRAP assay constitutes a substantial step forward in the ability to analyse the movement of RNPs in vitro.
source: Thus, the RAT-TRAP assay constitutes a substantial step forward in the ability to analyse the movement of RNPs in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of the new assay to previous methods.

claim: The data support a novel mechanism for multi-motor translocation based on the regulation of dynein processivity by discrete cargo-associated features.
source: Our data support a novel mechanism for multi-motor translocation based on the regulation of dynein processivity by discrete cargo-associated features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The same cargo species can interact with processive or non-processive dynein, with discrete cargo-associated features regulating the probability of switching between the two behaviours.
source: Collectively, our results support a novel model in which the same cargo species can interact with processive or non-processive dynein, with discrete cargo-associated features regulating the probability of switching between the two behaviours (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, with reference to a figure.

claim: The regulatory mechanisms underpinning sorting of RNPs in this system appear distinct from those of other well-studied bidirectional cargos, which involve the interplay of opposite polarity force-generating motors, such as dyneins and kinesins.
source: Thus, the regulatory mechanisms underpinning sorting of RNPs in this system appear distinct from those of other well-studied bidirectional cargos, which involve the interplay of opposite polarity force-generating motors, such as dyneins and kinesins (Shubeita et al., 2008; Ally et al., 2009; Soppina et al., 2009; Jolly and Gelfand, 2011; Reis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and comparison to published literature.

claim: Proteins recruited by the localisation signal could directly regulate the activity of the motor.
source: One possibility is that proteins recruited by the localisation signal directly regulate the activity of the motor.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The adaptor proteins Egl and BicD are candidates to directly regulate the activity of the motor.
source: Two candidates to serve such a role are the adaptor proteins Egl and BicD, which are associated only with the dynein-dynactin bound to the localisation signals (Bullock et al., 2006; Dix et al., 2013).

claim: The structure or rigidity of the RNA signal could play an architectural role in presenting dynein-dynactin to the microtubule in a manner that favours processive movement.
source: It is also conceivable that the structure or rigidity of the RNA signal plays an architectural role in presenting dynein-dynactin to the microtubule in a manner that favours processive movement.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

source: We show that RNPs frequently reverse when encountering the regions of microtubules bound by puncta of both MAPs studied, rigor kinesin and tau23.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

source: The behaviour of RNPs at MAPs is therefore highly reminiscent of that seen for individual, purified dynein-dynactin complexes in vitro (Dixit et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results to published literature.

claim: The number of dynein-dynactins associated with an RNP does not increase the probability of passing microtubule-associated obstacles.
source: Interestingly, comparison of the behaviour of the h RNA variants reveals that the number of dynein-dynactins associated with an RNP does not increase the probability of passing microtubule-associated obstacles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The ability of RNPs to reverse at MAPs may help them navigate to their destination in vivo.
source: The ability of RNPs to reverse at MAPs may help them navigate to their destination in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Reversals upon meeting an obstacle may facilitate encounters of RNPs with intersecting microtubules.
source: For example, reversals upon meeting an obstacle may facilitate encounters of RNPs with intersecting microtubules.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Switching of RNPs between microtubules could allow these complexes to explore alternative routes to their destination.
source: Switching of RNPs between microtubules, a behaviour we have observed when intersections occur in our in vitro assays (unpublished observations), could allow these complexes to explore alternative routes to their destination.
evidence: This is a speculation based on unpublished observations.

claim: Reversals of RNPs at a MAP may give dynein space to switch to a different lateral position on the same microtubule and thereby provide another opportunity to pass the obstacle following resumption of movement in the previous direction.
source: Reversals of RNPs at a MAP may also give dynein space to switch to a different lateral position on the same microtubule and thereby provide another opportunity to pass the obstacle following resumption of movement in the previous direction.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: RNPs can move on single microtubules and pass obstacles after multiple attempts.
source: Compatible with this notion, we see RNPs moving on single microtubules that can pass obstacles after multiple attempts (e.g., Figure 5D).

claim: Plus end encounters of RNPs always result in a reversal.
source: Our analysis of the behaviour of RNPs at microtubule ends indicates that plus end encounters always result in a reversal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The behaviour of RNPs at plus ends may be advantageous in a cellular environment by preventing detachment of RNPs at this point.
source: The behaviour may also be advantageous in a cellular environment by preventing detachment of RNPs at this point, an outcome that would necessitate a rebinding event before motion on the microtubule network can resume.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: The probability of changing directions is different at the minus end and the plus end of the microtubule.
source: Interestingly, a subset of RNPs undergoes pausing at the minus ends of microtubules, with a mean dwell time of ∼1 min for bidirectional complexes. These findings demonstrate that the probability of changing directions is different at the minus end and the plus end of the microtubule and that additional in vivo features, such as the γ-tubulin ring complex or other centrosome-associated factors, are not obligatory for long-term retention of RNPs at the minus end.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Additional in vivo features, such as the γ-tubulin ring complex or other centrosome-associated factors, are not obligatory for long-term retention of RNPs at the minus end.
source: Interestingly, a subset of RNPs undergoes pausing at the minus ends of microtubules, with a mean dwell time of ∼1 min for bidirectional complexes. These findings demonstrate that the probability of changing directions is different at the minus end and the plus end of the microtubule and that additional in vivo features, such as the γ-tubulin ring complex or other centrosome-associated factors, are not obligatory for long-term retention of RNPs at the minus end.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Intrinsic behaviours of RNPs upon reaching the minus end of the α/β-tubulin polymer may contribute to the dynein-dependent anchorage of RNAs in the vicinity of minus ends in vivo.
source: Intrinsic behaviours of RNPs upon reaching the minus end of the α/β-tubulin polymer may therefore contribute to the dynein-dependent anchorage of RNAs in the vicinity of minus ends in vivo (Delanoue and Davis, 2005).

source: Analysis of hΔLE, hWT, and hSL1x3 RNAs demonstrates that the probability of an RNP undergoing minus end pausing in vitro, as well as the duration of such events, is not influenced by the addition of more dynein-dynactins through localisation elements.

claim: Inhibition of Egl and BicD following translocation of localising RNAs to the apical cytoplasm of the embryo does not affect dynein-dependent anchorage.
source: This finding offers an explanation for why inhibition of Egl and BicD following translocation of localising RNAs to the apical cytoplasm of the embryo does not affect dynein-dependent anchorage (Delanoue and Davis, 2005).

source: One explanation for these findings is that the ability of dynein bound to localisation signals to walk processively off the minus end is antagonised by interactions with the microtubule mediated by non-processive dynein bound at other sites in the RNA.

claim: Features that promote bidirectional motion could assist in the retention of RNPs at minus ends.
source: Nonetheless, our data suggest more generally that features that promote bidirectional motion could assist in the retention of RNPs at minus ends.

source: Collectively, our analysis of encounters of RNPs with MAPs and microtubule ends raises the possibility that the co-existence of unidirectional or bidirectional modes of movement facilitates efficient navigation of an RNA population to its destination in vivo.

claim: Processive, unidirectional movement in the minus end direction could be beneficial for rapid, directional movement along regions of the microtubule that are not rich in MAPs.
source: Processive, unidirectional movement in the minus end direction could be beneficial for rapid, directional movement along regions of the microtubule that are not rich in MAPs.

source: Diffusive motion along microtubules may be valuable for movement of RNPs through an obstacle rich environment and could still contribute to asymmetric sorting as it is associated with long-term retention of complexes at microtubule minus ends.

source: This strategy appears analogous to that used by DNA enzymes and kinesins that depolymerise microtubules, which can employ one-dimensional diffusion to search for their specific target sites (Helenius et al., 2006; Gorman and Greene, 2008).

source: Our data lead to a model in which discrete cargo-associated features regulate motor processivity, a phenomenon that could not have been recapitulated using minimal motor elements coupled to artificial cargos.
